hints: Think what is needed to make charged particles move in one direction, what type of electrical supply gives constant positive and negative ends?
Remember the amino acids must be dissolved in something that keeps pH constant while conducting electricity, what solution does this?
Consider where you place the mixture at the start, what solid support holds the spot while ions migrate?
walkthrough:
Provide the driving force for migration**
Picture charged amino acids sitting still. They will only move if you apply an electric field. So you need a DC power supply or battery with clearly labelled + and - terminals connected to electrodes, forming a complete circuit. AC would keep swapping ends and get you nowhere.

Keep pH constant and conduct current**
The tank must contain a buffer solution which acts as the electrolyte. It conducts electricity between the electrodes and, crucially, it fixes the pH so each amino acid has a fixed, predictable charge throughout the run.

Support the sample spot**
The mixture is not just dropped in solution or it would diffuse. Place a small spot (X) of the amino acid mixture on moist filter paper, gel or agarose strip which dips into or contacts the buffer. When the voltage is on, cations move to the negative electrode and anions move to the positive electrode.

Final answer: Labelled diagram showing:
1. DC power supply / battery connected to positive and negative electrodes in a complete circuit.
2. Buffer solution / electrolyte in tank.
3. Filter paper / gel / agarose support with mixture spot (X) of amino acids applied.

hints: At a fixed buffer pH, some amino acids are cations and some are anions, which electrode will each type be attracted to?
If two ions have the same sign of charge, what decides which one moves further in the same time, think about size and magnitude of charge?
walkthrough:
Direction tells you the sign of the charge**
At the buffer pH each amino acid exists mainly as a cation $(+)$, anion $(-)$ or neutral / zwitterion. Opposites attract, so positively charged species migrate toward the negative electrode (cathode) and negatively charged species migrate toward the positive electrode (anode). Neutral species stay near the origin.

Distance tells you charge density**
How far they travel in a fixed time depends on charge magnitude and size. A highly charged, small ion experiences a larger electrical force per unit mass and less friction, so it moves faster and further. That is why separation works, different $M_r$ and different charge give different mobilities.

Final answer: Amino acids exist as differently charged species at a given pH. Direction of movement depends on sign of charge, cations move to negative electrode, anions move to positive electrode.
Distance moved / rate of movement depends on magnitude of charge and $M_r$ / size, greater charge and smaller size gives greater movement.

hints: Compare side chains from the Data Booklet, Asp has an extra $\text{-CH}_2\text{COOH}$ group while Val has only an alkyl group, at which pH will that extra acid group ionise?
walkthrough:
Spot the acidic R group**
Look at the Data Booklet. Val has a neutral hydrocarbon side chain $(\text{-CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2)$ which never gains or loses $\text{H}^{+}$. Asp has $\text{-CH}_2\text{COOH}$ in its side chain in addition to the normal $\alpha\text{-COOH}$ and $\alpha\text{-NH}_2$. That extra carboxylic acid is the key to separation.

Choose high pH to maximise charge difference**
At pH 12, well above all $pK_a$ values for acid groups, both carboxyl groups in Asp are $\text{COO}^{-}$ and the amino group is $\text{NH}_2$, giving overall $2-$. Val has only $\text{COO}^{-}$ and $\text{NH}_2$, giving $1-$. The more negative Asp is pulled more strongly to the positive electrode and moves further. pH 7 also works because Asp is $-1$ (anionic) while Val is $0$ (zwitterionic).

Final answer: buffer pH 12.0 (also acceptable pH 7.0 for good separation). At pH 12 Asp side chain $\text{-CH}_2\text{COOH}$ is deprotonated to $\text{-CH}_2\text{COO}^{-}$, so Asp has charge $2-$ while Val has charge $1-$, Asp moves further to positive electrode. At pH 7 Asp is anionic but Val is neutral / zwitterionic.

hints: Compare side chains, Lys has an extra $\text{-(CH}_2)_4\text{NH}_2$ group while Ser has only $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$, at which pH will that extra amine group stay protonated?
walkthrough:
Spot the basic R group**
Ser has a neutral $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ side chain which does not ionise in this range. Lys has $\text{-(CH}_2)_4\text{NH}_2$ in its side chain plus the normal $\alpha$ groups. That extra amine can pick up $\text{H}^{+}$ to become $\text{NH}_3^{+}$.

Choose low pH to maximise positive charge**
At pH 2, well below $pK_a$ values for amine groups, both nitrogens in Lys are protonated as $\text{NH}_3^{+}$ while $\text{COOH}$ stays un-ionised, giving overall $2+$. Ser has only one $\text{NH}_3^{+}$, giving $1+$. Lys is more strongly attracted to the negative electrode and moves further. pH 7 also separates because Lys is $+1$ while Ser is $0$.

Final answer: buffer pH 2.0 (also acceptable pH 7.0). At pH 2 Lys side chain is $(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{NH}_3^{+}$, so Lys has charge $2+$ while Ser has charge $1+$, Lys moves further to negative electrode. At pH 7 Lys is cationic but Ser is neutral / zwitterionic.

hints: Both have aromatic rings, but check the difference, Tyr has a phenol $\text{-OH}$ on the ring while Phe has only a hydrocarbon ring, when does phenol lose $\text{H}^{+}$?
walkthrough:
Find the only ionisable difference**
Both Tyr and Phe look similar with a benzyl type side chain. The crucial difference is Tyr has $\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH}$, a phenol group. Phe has $\text{-C}_6\text{H}_5$, just hydrocarbon, which cannot ionise. At pH 2 or 7 both amino acids have identical $\alpha$-group charges, so they would not separate.

Use very high pH to ionise the phenol**
Phenol is a very weak acid, it only deprotonates in strong alkali. At pH 12 the phenolic $\text{OH}$ loses $\text{H}^{+}$ to give $\text{O}^{-}$. So Tyr becomes $2-$ overall ($\alpha\text{-COO}^{-}$ plus phenoxide plus neutral $\text{NH}_2$) while Phe is only $1-$. Tyr therefore migrates further toward the positive electrode.

Final answer: buffer pH 12.0. At pH 12 Tyr phenolic group $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is deprotonated to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{O}^{-}$, so Tyr has charge $2-$ but Phe has charge $1-$, Tyr moves further / faster to positive electrode.

hints: Recall Gly is $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{COOH}$ and Ser is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)COOH}$, which $\text{COOH}$ joins to which $\text{NH}_2$ to make Gly-Ser?
Remember a peptide bond is a $\text{-CO-NH-}$ amide link formed by loss of water, and you must draw all atoms of that link, not just write CONH.
walkthrough:
Join COOH of Gly to NH2 of Ser**
The name Gly-Ser tells you the order. The $\text{C}$-terminus of Gly ($\text{H}_2\text{N-CH}_2\text{-COOH}$) condenses with the $\text{N}$-terminus of Ser ($\text{H}_2\text{N-CH(CH}_2\text{OH)-COOH}$) with loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$:
$$ \text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{NCH(CH}_2\text{OH)COOH} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CONHCH(CH}_2\text{OH)COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} $$

Display the peptide link fully**
Do not abbreviate the amide. Draw $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-NH-CH-}$ explicitly, showing the carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ and the $\text{N-H}$. Keep the free $\text{NH}_2$ on the Gly end, the free $\text{COOH}$ on the Ser end, and the Ser side chain $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ intact on the $\alpha$-carbon.

Final answer: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{-C(=O)-NH-CH(CH}_2\text{OH)-COOH}$ with peptide bond $\text{-CONH-}$ shown in full as $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$.
Structure: $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH}_2\text{-CO-NH-CH(CH}_2\text{OH)-COOH}$ with correct connectivity, Gly residue on left, Ser residue on right.

hints: Peak E is around $3200 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ in the broad hydrogen-bonded region, which single bonds to H absorb there?
Peaks F near $1650 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and G near $1050 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ are both carbon-oxygen bonds, which one is double and strong, and which one is single?
walkthrough:
Assign the high wavenumber peak E**
Peak E is at about $3200 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. From the Data Booklet this region is $\text{O-H}$ (alcohol, carboxylic acid, broad with hydrogen bonding) and $\text{N-H}$ (amine, amide). Gly-Ser contains $\text{-OH}$ in Ser side chain and $\text{COOH}$, plus $\text{-NH}_2$ and $\text{-NH-}$ (peptide), so E is $\text{O-H}$ or $\text{N-H}$.

Assign the carbonyl and single bond peaks F and G**
Peak F near $1650$ to $1700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the classic strong $\text{C=O}$ stretch of carboxylic acid and amide. Peak G near $1000$ to $1100 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the $\text{C-O}$ stretch of alcohol ($\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) and carboxylic acid. So F is $\text{C=O}$ and G is $\text{C-O}$.

Final answer: E is $\text{O-H}$ or $\text{N-H}$ stretch.
F is $\text{C=O}$ stretch and G is $\text{C-O}$ stretch.
